comments.author: @Mochiphoria
comments.text:
The taking over of public space seems to be the same trend cruise ships have. Previously-public or purchasable spaces (e.g. the adults-only pool and thermal suite on Princess) are being transformed into 'exclusive' perks tied to new cabin classes. Providing a quiet space for those in the club, but taking that quiet space away from the rest of the guests. Charging a premium for those cabins, even if most of the perks are services you won't use.

It's kind of the general trend of everything. Migrating existing features or services into a bundle that they can charge more for because it has more things, even if you still only wanted the 1 thing.

The new T-Mix plans from T-Mobile are another crazy example. Selling you 'choice' on the perks, but actually reducing the benefits. Instead of being opted into more perks than you use, you get to pick only the ones you want. Sounds like you're getting one-off add-ons and it should reduce the cost. But it's more like locking yourself out of all the other things, and still paying the premium for the right to choose. Things like Netflix cost multiple picks (credits), so you have to upgrade plans just to get enough picks to cover 1 thing (sounds a lot like upgrading to a bundle for the 1 thing in the bundle you want, only without the option to potentially use the other bundle items). And deals on new phones lock you out of using those picks on any other perks for the full 36 months of financing. So you have a plan with 3 lines, 1 pick per line. 1 person upgrades to a fancy phone. Now no one can redeem any other perk for 3 years.
I'm sure I don't fully understand that yet, and I have no intention of actually using it. But the dissonance between the real benefits and what they're advertising is wild.

The Delta/Centerion/Priority Pass crowding issue would be better controlled if they stripped access from Military Service members who have their annual Amex fees waived.
